skill.name: python-env
skill.description: Guides uv-based Python environment setup, dependency management, project configuration, testing workflows, and package publishing.
skill.summary: Manage reproducible Python projects and dependencies with uv.
skill.author: 0xDarkMatter

security_audit.summary: The audit confirmed one critical issue: SKILL.md recommends piping a remote installer directly into a shell. The other 87 findings are documentation examples or Markdown syntax without dangerous execution, access, or exfiltration intent.

remediation.issue: The uv installation instruction executes a remote response directly in a shell.
remediation.suggestion: Recommend an approved package manager, or download the installer, verify its checksum, inspect it, and execute it as a separate step.

static_findings.snippet: # Build sdist + wheel — uv has a native builder, no separate `build` install
# Dev tooling → dependency-groups (PEP 735). `uv add --dev <pkg>` writes here;
# `uv sync` installs it by default. Not shipped with the published package.
# Opt-in extras users install explicitly: `uv add "my-package[docs]"`
(`uv add` / `uv sync` / `uv run`) over the `uv pip` compatibility layer — it
manages `pyproject.toml` + a lockfile for you and is reproducible.
| Start a project | `uv init <name>` (app) · `uv init --package <name>` (installable, `src/` layout)
| Add dev dependency | `uv add --dev pytest ruff` |
| Run in project env | `uv run pytest` |
| Install a CLI tool | `uv tool install ruff` · one-shot: `uvx ruff` |
`uv init` creates `pyproject.toml`, pins a Python version, and prepares the
project for `uv add` / `uv sync`. The `--package` (src) layout is preferred for
`uv` creates and manages `.venv` automatically — you rarely activate it; just
uv run -- ruff check .      # `--` ends uv flag parsing
Never call bare `python` / `pytest` / `ruff` in a uv project — they may resolve
to a different interpreter. Always `uv run`.
Use `uv tool` / `uvx` for developer CLIs (ruff, pre-commit, httpie). Use
`uv add` only for things your code imports.
# Dev deps live here; `uv add --dev <pkg>` manages this group.
`uv pip` mirrors pip's interface for environments uv doesn't manage (a hand-made
venv, a legacy `requirements.txt`, CI that isn't uv-native). It does **not**
update `pyproject.toml` or the lockfile — prefer `uv add` / `uv sync` whenever
| Pin project Python | `uv init --python 3.12` or edit `requires-python` |
| Lock/resolve conflict | `uv lock --resolution=lowest-direct` to probe, then loosen bounds |
- `uv add` / `uv remove` / `uv sync` for project dependencies (not `uv pip install`)
- `uv run` to execute anything inside the project env
- `uv tool install` / `uvx` for standalone developer CLIs
- `uv pip` only for environments uv doesn't manage

content.value_statement: Python environments and dependency files can become slow, inconsistent, and difficult to reproduce. This skill provides practical uv workflows for setup, locking, testing, and publishing.
actual_capabilities: Creates application and package projects with uv.
Adds, removes, locks, and synchronizes Python dependencies.
Runs Python, tests, and developer tools inside managed environments.
Provides pyproject.toml patterns for applications, libraries, and tool configuration.
Explains workspaces, private indexes, Git dependencies, and local dependencies.
Guides package builds, TestPyPI checks, releases, and trusted publishing.
limitations: Requires the uv command-line tool and permission to change project files.
Does not validate package trust, licenses, or vulnerability status.
Publishing steps require repository and PyPI configuration outside this skill.
Examples need adaptation for each operating system, index, and project policy.

use_cases.title: Start a Python project
use_cases.description: Create a reproducible project with a suitable layout, Python version, dependencies, and development tools.
use_cases.target_user: Python developers starting a new application or library

use_cases.title: Modernize dependency workflows
use_cases.description: Replace manual virtual environments and pip commands with uv project commands and a committed lockfile.
use_cases.target_user: Maintainers updating an existing Python repository

use_cases.title: Prepare a package release
use_cases.description: Configure package metadata, build artifacts, test installation through TestPyPI, and use trusted publishing.

prompt_templates.title: Create a basic environment
prompt_templates.prompt: Set up this Python project with uv. Use Python [version], add [dependencies], and explain each proposed file change.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for an existing folder

prompt_templates.title: Configure development tools
prompt_templates.prompt: Add pytest, Ruff, and mypy to this uv project. Update pyproject.toml with practical defaults and run the appropriate checks.

prompt_templates.title: Migrate from pip
prompt_templates.prompt: Migrate this repository from requirements files to a uv project workflow. Preserve constraints, separate development dependencies, and describe compatibility risks.

prompt_templates.title: Design a release workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a secure uv-based release workflow for this package. Include builds, TestPyPI validation, versioning, GitHub Actions, and PyPI trusted publishing.

output_examples.input: Create a Python 3.12 API project with FastAPI, pytest, and Ruff.
output_examples.output: The response proposes a package layout, initializes Python 3.12, separates runtime and development dependencies, and lists validation steps.

output_examples.input: Convert this requirements-based project to uv.
output_examples.output: The response maps direct dependencies into project metadata, creates development groups, generates a lockfile, and notes remaining legacy constraints.
The response checks metadata, changelog, tests, build artifacts, TestPyPI installation, release tags, and trusted publishing configuration.

best_practices: Commit the lockfile and use frozen synchronization in continuous integration.
Review dependency sources and version changes before installing or upgrading packages.
Use PyPI trusted publishing instead of storing long-lived upload tokens.
anti_patterns: Do not pipe remote installation scripts directly into a shell.
Do not mix bare Python commands with uv-managed project commands.
Do not publish artifacts before testing their contents and installation.

faq.question: What does this skill require?
faq.answer: It requires the uv command-line tool and a writable Python project directory.

faq.question: Does it replace pip?
faq.answer: It prefers uv project commands but documents uv pip for legacy environments and requirements files.

faq.question: Can it create virtual environments?
faq.answer: Yes. uv creates project environments automatically and can also create standalone virtual environments.

faq.question: Does it support monorepos?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes uv workspace patterns for multiple packages that share one environment and lockfile.

faq.question: Can it publish packages?
faq.answer: It guides building, TestPyPI validation, versioning, and PyPI publishing. External account and repository setup remain required.

faq.question: How does it handle secrets?
faq.answer: It recommends trusted publishing and environment-based credentials. Users must protect local configuration and avoid committing tokens.
